title: Why QR Codes Have Three Corner Squares

voice.note: PREVIEW ONLY. The channel's approved voice is Edge en-US-EmmaMultilingualNeural; re-narrate with --voice edge before any publishing review.
voice.wordTiming: line timing measured per take; word timing inside a line estimated (energy envelope, punctuation-snapped pauses, syllable weights)

lines: Those three QR squares aren't decoration.
They tell the scanner where to look.
Denso Wave released the QR Code in 1994, and QR means quick response.
The corner marks are position detection patterns. Finding them made high-speed reading possible.
Why squares? The team said that pattern was least likely to appear on business forms.
They surveyed flyers, magazines and cardboard boxes for the rarest black-and-white ratio.
That rare ratio lets a scanner orient the code from any angle.

traceability.purpose: Separate the three squares from the data visually: everything else disappears, so 'not decoration' is seen, not just heard. Plants the empty fourth corner.

evidence.claim: The developers added positional information indicating that a code is present and should be read.
evidence.quote: adding positional information indicating the existence of a code to be read
evidence.source: DENSO WAVE — History of QR Code

evidence.claim: The three finder patterns sit at the upper left, upper right and lower left corners.
evidence.quote: at the upper left, upper right and lower left corners of the QR code image

traceability.purpose: Show what 'tell the scanner where to look' means: a reader's scan lines sweep a cluttered package, and its marks lock onto exactly the three squares, then join them.

evidence.quote: adding positional information indicating the existence of a code to be read

traceability.purpose: Anchor the invention in time and name: the year ruler lands on 1994 as it is spoken, and the letters QR unfold into the words they stand for.

evidence.claim: Denso Wave, then a division of Denso Corporation, announced the release of the QR Code in 1994.
evidence.quote: In 1994, DENSO WAVE (then a division of DENSO CORPORATION) announced the release of its QR Code
evidence.source: DENSO WAVE — History of QR Code

evidence.claim: QR stands for quick response, reflecting a development focus on high-speed reading.
evidence.quote: The QR in the name stands for quick response
evidence.source: DENSO WAVE — History of QR Code

traceability.purpose: Name the corner marks and show their structure: one pattern lifts out as three stacked layers (dark, light, dark), then the reader finds all three and the data is read in one fast sweep.

evidence.claim: The square position detection marks made high-speed reading possible.
evidence.quote: By incorporating these marks into their code, high-speed reading became possible
evidence.source: DENSO WAVE — History of QR Code

evidence.claim: The three finder patterns sit at the upper left, upper right and lower left corners.
evidence.quote: at the upper left, upper right and lower left corners of the QR code image

traceability.purpose: Make 'least likely to appear on business forms' concrete: a template of the nested-square pattern searches a busy form and every square-ish feature fails to match; the team's words appear verbatim.

evidence.claim: Masahiro Hara said square marks were chosen because that pattern was least likely to appear on business forms.
evidence.quote: it was the pattern least likely to appear on various business forms and the like
evidence.source: DENSO WAVE — History of QR Code

evidence.claim: A similar-looking mark near the code could be mistaken for a position detection pattern, so the pattern had to be unique.
evidence.quote: their position detection patterns had to be truly unique
evidence.source: DENSO WAVE — History of QR Code

traceability.purpose: Show what 'black-and-white ratio' means: a scan line turns printed matter into runs of black and white; then the line crosses the corner pattern and its runs measure exactly 1:1:3:1:1.

evidence.claim: The team surveyed the ratio of white to black areas in printing on fliers, magazines and cardboard boxes.
evidence.quote: an exhaustive survey of the ratio of white to black areas in pictures and symbols printed on fliers, magazines, cardboard boxes
evidence.source: DENSO WAVE — History of QR Code

evidence.claim: The least-used black-and-white ratio on printed matter, 1:1:3:1:1, set the widths of the position detection patterns.
evidence.quote: came up with the least used ratio of black and white areas on printed matter. This ratio was 1:1:3:1:1
evidence.source: DENSO WAVE — History of QR Code

traceability.purpose: Prove the payoff: the code turns to different angles while the scan line through the corner keeps reading the same 1:1:3:1:1 runs; three found corners plus the empty one fix which way is up, and the code settles upright.

evidence.claim: Searching for this unique ratio lets a reader determine the code's orientation at any scanning angle.
evidence.quote: the orientation of their code could be determined regardless of the angle of scanning
evidence.source: DENSO WAVE — History of QR Code

evidence.source: DENSO WAVE — History of QR Code
